documents.content:
Cracker Barrel shareholders have voted to retain CEO Julie Felss Masino, despite a controversial logo redesign in August that impacted sales and ultimately led to the chain swiftly reversing course\.

Director Gilbert Davila resigned after failing to secure re-election\.

Davila, who joined the board in 2020, also serves as president and CEO of DMI Consulting, a multicultural marketing firm, and was responsible for reviewing Cracker Barrel’s advertising\. His re-election was opposed by influential shareholder advisory firms, Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis\.

Cracker Barrel CEO Julie Felss Masino said the redesign had nothing to do with ideology \(REUTERS\)

The vote followed a concerted campaign by activist investor Sardar Biglari, who had pushed for the removal of both Masino and Davila\. Biglari, chairman and CEO of Biglari Holdings Inc\., which owns Steak ‘n Shake, holds a 3% stake in Cracker Barrel\. He stated in a letter to investors earlier this month: \"Our campaign is about saving Cracker Barrel from a board and management team that are out of touch with Cracker Barrel’s customer base\.\"

Masino, a former executive at Taco Bell and Starbucks, was appointed CEO in July 2023 with a mandate to innovate and attract new customers to the chain’s 660 restaurants across 43 states\. Her initiatives included introducing updated menu items, such as Hashbrown Casserole Shepherd’s Pie, to boost dinner traffic, and remodelling the company’s traditionally antique-filled restaurants with lighter walls and more comfortable seating\.

However, her decision in August to simplify the chain’s logo sparked widespread backlash\. Loyal customers expressed dismay that the new design omitted Cracker Barrel’s long-standing mascot – an overall-clad man leaning on a barrel – and the words \"Old Country Store\.\" The restaurant redesigns also met with significant resistance\.

Cracker Barrel reinstated its original logo within a week and suspended restaurant remodelling in early September\. Despite these retractions, the controversy is projected to have a lasting impact on sales\. The company forecast a 7 to 8% decline in store traffic for its fiscal first quarter, with a potential 4 to 7% drop for the full fiscal year 2026, which commenced on August 2\.

November 20, 2025

\(AP\) — Cracker Barrel shareholders voted Thursday to keep company CEO Julie Felss Masino in place despite a debacle over the company’s logo that continues to hurt its sales\. But one of the company’s directors, Gilbert Davila, resigned from Cracker Barrel’s board Thursday after preliminary results indicated that shareholders rejected his reelection\. Sardar Biglari, a longtime Cracker Barrel shareholder who also runs Steak ‘n Shake, was among those pressing to oust Masino and Davila\. Cracker Barrel angered fans in August when it announced plans to simplify its logo and remodel its antique-filled stores\. The company has since backtracked on those plans but said it expects its sales to be down this year\.

FILE – This aerial image taken with a drone shows a Cracker Barrel restaurant in Binghamton, N\.Y\., Aug\. 23, 2025\. \(AP Photo/Ted Shaffrey, File\)

## FULL STORY

Cracker Barrel shareholders voted Thursday to keep company CEO Julie Felss Masino in place despite a debacle over the company’s logo that continues to hurt its sales\.

But one of the company’s directors, Gilbert Davila, resigned from Cracker Barrel’s board Thursday after preliminary results indicated that shareholders rejected his reelection\.

Davila, who joined Cracker Barrel’s board in 2020, is the president and CEO of DMI Consulting, a multicultural marketing firm\. He reviewed Cracker Barrel’s advertising as part of his role on the board\. Two influential shareholder advisory firms, Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis, had recommended against Davila’s reelection ahead of the vote\.

Sardar Biglari, a longtime Cracker Barrel shareholder and activist investor, was among those pressing for the ouster of Masino and Davila\. Biglari is the chairman and CEO of Biglari Holdings Inc\., a San Antonio, Texas-based company that owns Steak ‘n Shake\. He also owns 3% of Cracker Barrel’s shares\.

“Our campaign is about saving Cracker Barrel from a board and management team that are out of touch with Cracker Barrel’s customer base,” Biglari said in a letter sent earlier this month to Cracker Barrel investors\.

Cracker Barrel hired Masino, a longtime Taco Bell and Starbucks executive, in July 2023\. She was chosen for her record as an innovator, with the hope that she would attract new customers to Cracker Barrel, which operates 660 restaurants in 43 states\.

Masino introduced updated menu items, like Hashbrown Casserole Shepherd’s Pie, to increase Cracker Barrel’s dinnertime traffic\. She also started remodeling the company’s dark, antique-filled restaurants, lightening the walls and installing more comfortable seating\.

But her decision in August to simplify the chain’s logo had disastrous consequences\. Fans didn’t like that the new logo didn’t include Cracker Barrel’s longtime mascot, an overall-clad man leaning on a barrel, or the words “Old Country Store\.” They also rebelled against the store redesigns\.

Cracker Barrel reversed course a week later, saying it would keep its old logo\. In early September, the company also suspended the remodeling of its restaurants\.

The moves could hurt Cracker Barrel’s sales well into next year\. Cracker Barrel said in September that store traffic would likely be down between 7% and 8% in its fiscal first quarter and could decline 4% to 7% for the full 2026 fiscal year, which began Aug\. 2\.

# Who is David Deno? Restaurant veteran named Cracker Barrel’s new CEO

## Cracker Barrel appoints industry veteran David Deno as new CEO amid sales challenges and backlash over its rebranding efforts\. Deno will succeed Julie Felss Masino on August 10 to lead company growth and transition\.

July 28, 2026 19:55 IST

Cracker Barrel Old Country Store has named restaurant industry veteran David Deno as its new chief executive officer after a difficult year due to weak sales and public backlash\.

Deno, the former CEO of Bloomin’ Brands, the parent company of Outback Steakhouse and Carrabba’s Italian Grill, will take over on August 10\. He succeeds Julie Felss Masino, who became CEO in July 2023\. Masino will step down from the board but stay on as an advisor until October 9 to help with the transition\.

“David brings decades of experience across the restaurant and retail industries,with a strong track record of leading businesses through growth and a demonstrated commitment to operational excellence,” said Carl Berquist, independent chairman of the Cracker Barrel board\.

## Who is David Deno?

Deno has worked in the restaurant and retail industry for more than 40 years\. He was CEO of Bloomin’ Brands from 2019 to 2024\. Before that, he spent 15 years at Yum\! Brands, where he served as chief financial officer and chief operating officer\. He also worked as CFO of Pizza Hutand started his career at Burger King\. He is currently a board member at Krispy Kreme and Panera Brands\.

ALSO READ

Julie Felss Masino became Cracker Barrel’s president and CEO in July 2023\. Before joining the company, she was president, international, at Taco Bell from 2020 to 2023\. She has also worked at Fisher-Price, Sprinkles Cupcakes and Starbucks\. She will leave the CEO role on August 10 and remain an advisor until October\.

## Why did Cracker Barrel face backlash?

Masino faced criticism in 2025 after Cracker Barrel announced a major makeover plan\. The company introduced a new logo and updated restaurant interiors\. The new logo removed “Uncle Herschel,” the man leaning on a wooden barrel, for the first time in 48 years\.

ALSO READ

The change drew criticism from conservative commentators, MAGA supporters and some political leaders\. They said the company was moving away from its traditional Southern identity\. The criticism also followed earlier complaints about Cracker Barrel’s Pride Month posts and its diversity, equity and inclusion \(DEI\) policies\.

Media personality Collin Rugg called the new logo depressing, while the conservative account End Wokeness said company leaders should face charges for a “crime against humanity\.” Others criticized the outrage\. Former Ohio State Senator Nina Turner said people were focusing on a restaurant logo while many Americans were struggling with housing, groceries and medical bills\.

President Donald Trump also urged the company to bring back the old logo\. “They got a Billion Dollars worth of free publicity if they play their cards right\. Very tricky to do, but a great opportunity\. Have a major News Conference today\. Make Cracker Barrel a WINNER again,” Trump wrote on Truth Social\. He had earlier asked the company to “go back to the old logo, admit a mistake based on customer response \(the ultimate Poll\), and manage the company better than ever before\.”

A beloved Alabama breakfast restaurant owned by Cracker Barrel has closed for good, as the company struggles with ongoing fallout from conservative outrage over its logo\.

The venue, part of the Maple Street Biscuit Company chain, appeared to have been abruptly shuttered after six years in downtown Homewood\.

“This location is permanently closed,” read a sign on the door on Monday, reported by local CBS affiliate WIAT\.

“Thank you to our amazing team and to the wonderful Homewood community that has supported us over the years\.”

The restaurant, on the corner of 18th Street and 28th Avenue, is the latest in a string of Maple Street closures that have roiled the chain, with Cracker Barrel confirming last September “that 14 locations would be impacted by the closures during fiscal 2026,” Fox Business reported\.

\"We appreciate the continued patronage of the many guests who have dined with Maple Street at these 14 locations over recent years and thank our team members for their passionate dedication to Maple Street and focus on delivering fantastic guest experiences day in and day out,\" a Cracker Barrel spokesperson told Fox Business at the time\.

The spokesperson confirmed those 14 restaurants had already been axed, meaning the Homewood shuttering is an additional closure\.

Maple Street Biscuit Company is a brunch chain beloved for its flaky biscuits, fried chicken and house-made sauces, which it touts as “comfort food with a modern twist\.”

One of its signature biscuit dishes is ‘The Squawking Goat,’ featuring hand-breaded fried chicken breast, a fried goat cheese medallion and pepper jelly, which has appeared on Food Network’s ‘Guilty Pleasures\.’

Maple Street was founded by Gus Evans and Scott Moore in Jacksonville, Florida, in 2012, and quickly became a hit, rapidly expanding into other states over the next decade\.

Maple Street Biscuit Company is a brunch chain beloved for its “comfort food with a modern twist” \(Carmen K\. Sisson/Adobe Stock\)

Cracker Barrel, a highly popular southern-themed restaurant chain, took note of the new arrival, snapping up Maple Street in October 2019 in a deal worth $36 million\.

It was still expanding as recently as 2023, when Maple Street announced Ohio would be its 10th state of operations\.

However, Cracker Barrel hit rocky financial headwinds last August following a disastrous decision to revamp and simplify its longstanding logo, which inadvertently became a new culture war flashpoint as conservatives raged against the redesign\.

Influencers and MAGA Republicans branded the firm’s decision to ditch Uncle Herschel on the Cracker Barrel logo as “woke,” with thousands of online memes tearing into the company’s new look being posted after the news of the change broke\.

The backlash was so extreme that the company’s CEO admitted that she felt as though she had been “fired by America\.”

MAGA influencer Benny Johnson was among those melting down over Cracker Barrel's redesigned logo last August\. \(Benny Johnson/X\)

Cracker Barrel’s redesign caused it to lose $94 million in a single day, and its stock price plunged to $54\.50\. That meant the company’s stock price had plummeted by 7\.15 percent, although it had rebounded from a 15 percent drop earlier in the day\.

Even President Donald Trump weighed in on Cracker Barrel’s proposed new look, telling the company that it “should go back to the old logo” and “admit a mistake based on customer response \(the ultimate poll\)\.”

Cracker Barrel subsequently reversed its rebrand plans and confirmed that its stores would retain their iconic country theme\.

A month later, when it confirmed it was axing 14 Maple Street stores, the company simply said they “fell short of its financial expectations,” Fox Business reported\.

Dozens of Maple Street stores remain open in Florida, Texas, Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, Kentucky, and Ohio\.

# Who Is Julie Masino? Cracker Barrel CEO Stepping Down After Rebranding Backlash

Cracker Barrel is entering a new chapter as Julie Masino steps down and restaurant industry veteran David Deno prepares to lead the iconic chain through its next phase\. X/ CrackerBarrel

Cracker Barrel is changing leadership after announcing that CEO Julie Masino will step down, marking the end of a tenure defined by ambitious modernization efforts that divided customers and investors alike\. The restaurant chain confirmed Monday that Masino will be replaced by former Bloomin' Brands CEO David Deno, with the transition beginning in August\.

The leadership shake-up comes after months of criticism surrounding Cracker Barrel's rebranding strategy, including a controversial logo redesign that sparked customer backlash and briefly wiped nearly $100 million off the company's market value\. While the company has not explicitly linked Masino's departure to the controversy, the move has renewed questions about whether its attempt to modernize one of America's most recognizable restaurant brands went too far\.

### The company said that Masino will remain in an advisory role until Oct\. 9 to help ensure a smooth leadership transition\. In its announcement, Cracker Barrel focused on the transition rather than offering a reason for her exit, while introducing Deno as the executive tasked with leading the next phase of the company's strategy\.

### Who Is Julie Masino?

Julie Masino joined Cracker Barrel as CEO in 2023 after serving as president of Taco Bell's international operations, where she helped oversee global restaurant expansion and brand development\. When she arrived at Cracker Barrel, Masino made it clear that she wanted to modernize the company's image and attract younger customers\. Part of that effort included updating restaurants, refreshing menu offerings, and repositioning the brand for a changing restaurant industry\.

### One of Masino's most visible initiatives was an effort to refresh Cracker Barrel's identity\. In 2025, the company unveiled a redesigned logo that removed the familiar illustration of founder Dan Evins' Uncle Herschel sitting in a wicker chair beside a barrel, an image that had been closely associated with the brand for decades\.

The broader modernization strategy also included menu changes and updates to the customer experience, with Masino previously saying the restaurant was \"not as relevant as we once were\.\" The goal was to broaden Cracker Barrel's appeal beyond its traditional customer base while maintaining its reputation for Southern comfort food and country hospitality\.

### Why Did Customers React So Strongly?

The logo redesign quickly became one of the company's biggest public relations challenges\. Many longtime customers argued that removing Uncle Herschel stripped away part of Cracker Barrel's identity and ignored the nostalgia that had made the chain successful\.

Criticism spread rapidly across social media, with customers accusing the company of abandoning its heritage in an attempt to appear more modern\. The backlash was so significant that Cracker Barrel eventually reversed course and announced it would restore the original logo\. The controversy also weighed on investor confidence, with reports indicating the company's market value fell by nearly $100 million during the public reaction\.

### What Did Cracker Barrel Say About the Leadership Change?

Cracker Barrel announced that David Deno will become its next CEO beginning Aug\. 10\. In a statement, Deno praised the company's heritage while signaling that he intends to build on its strengths\. \"Cracker Barrel is a truly iconic American brand, defined by its unique combination of warm country hospitality, timeless appeal and deep connection with guests across generations,\" Deno said\. \"I am honored to lead the Cracker Barrel team and look forward to unlocking the full potential of this remarkable brand\.\"

### David Deno most recently served as CEO of Bloomin' Brands, the parent company of Outback Steakhouse, along with several other restaurant chains\. His experience leading large restaurant brands made him an attractive choice as Cracker Barrel looks to rebuild customer confidence while navigating a competitive dining environment\.

### What Challenges Does the New CEO Face?

Deno inherits several major priorities, including: Rebuilding customer trust after the branding controversy; Balancing modernization with Cracker Barrel's traditional identity; Increasing restaurant traffic; Managing inflation and higher operating costs; Keeping the brand competitive while preserving its loyal customer base\.

Finding that balance will likely determine whether Cracker Barrel can successfully evolve without alienating the customers who helped build its reputation\.

# Cracker Barrel CEO Julie Masino Steps Down After 'Woke' Logo Controversy

Cracker Barrel’s CEO, Julie Masino, is stepping down, the restaurant announced on Monday, nearly a year after the company faced a political storm over proposed branding updates\.

## Backlash over logo change

In August 2024, Cracker Barrel unveiled an updated logo that removed Uncle Herschel, the overall-clad man leaning against a barrel in the original logo\. Critics on social media denounced the rustic chain as “woke” and “sterile and soulless”\. Donald Trump weighed in, posting “WTF is wrong with Cracker Barrel?\!” and demanding the company “admit a mistake”\. The company quickly reverted to its old logo\.

Masino, who became CEO in 2023, told rightwing commentator Glenn Beck in December that she felt “fired by America” after the controversy\.

—

## Transition and market reaction

Cracker Barrel’s stock dropped nearly 3% after the announcement of Masino’s departure\. New CEO David Deno will take over on 10 August, with Masino staying until October to assist the transition\. “Cracker Barrel is a truly iconic American brand, defined by its unique combination of warm country hospitality, timeless appeal, and deep connection with guests across generations,” Deno said in a statement\.

## Broader trend of brand boycotts

Masino’s exit is the latest fallout from social media-driven backlash against brands perceived as appealing to certain political ideals\. The Harris Poll found that a quarter of Americans have changed shopping habits to align with their morals, with 50% of Democrats and 41% of Republicans stopping shopping at stores opposing their political views\. In 2023, Target and Bud Light both saw sales declines after pride-related campaigns\. Conversely, Target was dropped as a sponsor from Minneapolis’s annual pride festival after ending its diversity, equality and inclusion policies\.

Not all boycotts succeed: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey performed strongly at the global box office despite criticism from Elon Musk and others over a “woke” cast\.

## History of discrimination

Cracker Barrel has a record of discriminatory practices\. In 1991, it blocked hiring of LGBTQ\+ workers and dismissed 11 staff, later reversing the policy\. In 2004, it paid $8\.7m to settle allegations from Black customers denied service and Black employees given more “back of house” assignments compared with white counterparts\.

# Cracker Barrel replaces CEO less than a year after failed remodel, new logo

A Cracker Barrel sign featuring the old logo hangs outside of a restaurant on August 27, 2025 in Florida City, Florida\. \(Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images\)

The chief executive officer who was in charge at Cracker Barrel during its disastrous remodeling plan that included an attempt to update the logo and was quickly reversed in the wake of public backlash has been replaced\.

Big picture view:

David Deno will take the reins of the southern food restaurant chain in two weeks, the company announced Monday\. Deno will take over as CEO at Cracker Barrel after serving in the same role at Bloomin’ Brands, which manages several restaurant chains including Outback Steakhouse and Carrabba’s Italian Grill, between 2019 and 2024, according to the statement announcing the move\.

Cracker Barrel announces David Deno would take over as CEO on August 10, 2026\. \(Source: Cracker Barrel\)

By the numbers:

\"\(Deno\) brings decades of experience across the restaurant and retail industries, with a strong track record of leading businesses through growth and a demonstrated commitment to operational excellence, guest experience, and team member engagement,\" said Carl Berquist, who chairs the Cracker Barrel Board\.

The backstory:

While current CEO Julie Masino will step down from that role when Deno takes over on August 10, she will hold an advisory position until October 9 to help with the transition\. Masino had been in charge last year when the company revealed plans to roll out its \"modern remodel design\" to hundreds of its locations\.

At the time, only four of its 660 restaurants had implemented the remodel, but the change made national news and received harsh criticism from many customers\. Cracker Barrel quickly reversed course and assured its patrons that restaurants that had not received the new look would not get it and that the company would keep its \"Old Timer\" logo\.

What they're saying:

Dig deeper:

Cracker Barrel detailed its coming change at the top less than a week after saying it sold the Maple Street Biscuit Company brand and the assets tied to 35 locations to Biscuit Belly, LLC\. The remaining 16 Maple Street restaurants would be shuttered\.

Separately, Cracker Barrel completed a sale-leaseback deal for 26 company-owned locations that was expected to net roughly $77 million for the company as it looked to shed debt\.

# Cracker Barrel CEO Julie Masino resigns amid online threats over rebrand

A logo tweak spiraled into a threatening backlash, forcing a CEO to seek company paid protection and abandon a modernization plan\.

The New York Cracker Barrel announcement pointed to a new twist in the company’s history: Chief executive Julie Masino is leaving the company, but her departure is accompanied by security funded by the company after the public uproar over the branding last year\.

In essence, the issue is that Masino needs extra protection because of an online attack directed at the company over the logo change\.

If there is a sign of our era of anger, it’s this: a leader who had previously gone largely unnoticed became the target of online attacks for trying to steer the brand in a new direction, which critics see as undermining the establishment’s cultural identity\.

Americans are angry about the economy and politics, but feel they cannot control large forces\. So any symbolic action can become a trigger for outrage – even if the target did not cause harm, as in the case of a random woman who happened to be in frame with her boss at a Coldplay concert and received death threats\.

Big brands, sensitive to public pressure, have become easy targets of disappointment\. It’s easier to gather likes on social media, complaining about the logo, than to build housing\. People stage outrage flash mobs over Cracker Barrel’s logo change, Bud Light’s post featuring a transgender influencer, and Target’s backpedaling on DEI\.

> *This gives the public a sense of agency\. The brand will respond to stakeholders’ demands and pressure faster than a member of Congress\.*
> 
> – Allison Taylor

After this, anti-cultural forces from the right wing pushed the anti-woke movement, and companies backed away from previous commitments when Trump returned to the White House\.

In this context Cracker Barrel emerged\. Influential right-wing activists like Robby Starbuck, Benny Johnson and an investor in Steak ’n Shake stirred up anger and the unfolding of criticism\.

It was around this time that Masino became CEO in 2023 to attract a younger audience, as the older customer base stopped regularly visiting the venues; the brand was increasingly out of touch compared with competitors like Chili’s and Texas Roadhouse\.

Cracker Barrel felt the pressure from competitors, but Masino rolled out an active renewal strategy: improvements to dining rooms and changes to the menu\. Yet the first four quarters of sales growth did not stave off a crisis after the company unveiled the new logo in August last year\.

The change included a minimalist logo, while removing the barrel and the “old-timer” image – yet this did not stop the wave of outrage\. At the time some conservative figures argued that this demonstrated a “radical left lobby\.”

> *This is not about a specific restaurant chain – it doesn’t matter – but about creating mass pressure against companies that consider any move that might seem “wokification\.”*
> 
> – Christopher Rufo

A few days later Cracker Barrel reversed the new course, brought back the Old Timer logo, and canceled plans to remodel the restaurants\.

Masino went on a public apology tour: she appeared on the podcast of conservative host Glenn Beck, whose show was framed as an “honest confession\.”

“I want people to love this place,” Masino said, fighting back tears\. Beck leaned in and shook her hand\.

This story reflects a deeper context: the rage spiral around Cracker Barrel was not just about the logo, but about the way culture discusses changes in the corporate world and responds to political and economic anxieties through symbols and brands\.

# A bad logo could cost you your job

Cracker Barrel old vs new logo\.

On 20 August, 2025, American restaurant chain Cracker Barrel released its new identity to the world, and what followed was a rebrand backlash for the ages\. At the centre of the controversy was a new logo design which sported a minimalist aesthetic and, more pressingly, the erasure of iconic old-timer good ol' Uncle Herschel\. Critics demanded justice be served, and at last, in the year of our Lord 2026, it cometh\.

After a messy fallout, Cracker Barrel's CEO Julie Felss Masino is stepping down from her role, soon to be replaced by the CEO of Bloomin' Brands, David Deno\. Regardless of how you feel about the controversial rebrand, one pressing issue has reared its head\. A bad logo can now cost you your job\.

\(Image credit: Cracker Barrel\)

## What's woke got to do with it?

Cracker Barrel's rebrand was criticised for a number of reasons – some more measured than others\. Many saw the new minimalist design as a sterilisation of the brand's quirky heritage, while others claimed it was the victim of the 'blandification' epidemic spreading across the design world\. Then MAGA joined the conversation\.\.\.

Soon cries of 'woke' were being hollered across social media as notorious MAGA figureheads such as mini Donald Trump Jr\. lambasted the brand for its new logo\. Over on X, Floridian Republican Byron Donalds wrote, \"No one asked for this woke rebrand\. It’s time to Make Cracker Barrel Great Again\.” Woke War Room \(yes, that's a real account\) added, \"Cracker Barrel’s new logo isn’t an accident – it’s CEO Julie Felss Masino’s project\. She scrapped a beloved American aesthetic and replaced it with sterile, soulless branding,\" directly pointing the blame at the CEO herself\.

\(Image credit: SOPA Images via Getty Images\)

## Facing the fallout

Despite Cracker Barrel's CEO revealing the surprising reason behind its controversial rebrand, critics were still unconvinced\. Turns out the ol' \"highway visibility\" excuse wasn't enough for Uncle Herschel purists who staunchly opposed the new look\.

In August 2025, the critics won, and Cracker Barrel's old logo was reinstated\. Many internet whingers were filled with a sense of pride, but for some it wasn't enough – they needed to know it would never happen again\.

That brings us to today, where CEO Julie Felss Masino has officially stepped down from the company\. In her place steps David Deno with the patriotically worded introduction: “Cracker Barrel is a truly iconic American brand, defined by its unique combination of warm country hospitality, timeless appeal, and deep connection with guests across generations\.” Translation: Cracker Barrel will return to its traditional, all-American roots\.

\(Image credit: Cracker Barrel\)

## Is a bad logo worth expulsion?

In short, no\. The nature of design is so subjective that a failed rebrand shouldn't cost someone their career, but clearly the Cracker Barrel controversy was much more than a simple case of bad design\. For such an inoffensive, corporate rebrand, the politically charged backlash was unprecedented – a rebrand is always going to ruffle feathers, but no one could've predicted the onslaught directed at Cracker Barrel\.

Ever since MAGA media got hold of this story, Masino has had a target on her back, naturally making her the scapegoat of the situation\. Was it a poorly executed, uninspired rebrand? I would argue yes, but placing the blame solely on the former CEO is, in my opinion, unwarranted\. In some respects, it's likely easier for Masino to go down with the ship, but it highlights a much more sinister issue with branding backlash\.

Social media isn't afraid to get personal\. In the information age, angry consumers no longer need to shake their fists at a faceless corporation – a quick Google search can tell you exactly who to blame\. A failed rebrand is no longer just bad design; it's a cultural attack, a desecration of tradition engineered to make *you* angry\. A face to direct one's rage is a new level of validation, especially when it results in the dethroning of a CEO\. Yet, that doesn't make it right\.

For more branding insight, take a look at why logo backlashes aren't really about designor check out why it's time to stop judging rebrands so quickly\.
